narrative:
Your hands remember seed grain, wet earth, and the terrible arithmetic of a pantry in late winter, better than they remember anything a story would call heroic. You've known since you were young that Aldenmoor was not going to be the whole of your life. Knowing it and actually waking up on the morning it becomes true turn out to be very different things.

The house is quiet in the particular way a house gets when everyone in it is awake and pretending not to be, out of consideration for whoever isn't ready yet.

narrative:
Your mother, Aveline, finds you before you finish deciding how to find her - she always does, some instinct older than either of you can explain. She doesn't cry. She decided a long time ago that crying was a luxury a farm with one fewer pair of hands couldn't afford this morning, and she's holding to that decision through visible effort.

@Aveline: Well. Today, then. I'd hoped you'd forget to actually go through with it, if I'm honest. Foolish of me. You never forgot anything you set your mind to, not once, not since you were small enough to carry.

narrativeVariants.flags.civilian_departure_mood == 'sister:
Your mother, Aveline, finds the two of you together, which seems to settle something in her posture that had been tight since before you woke. She doesn't cry. She decided a long time ago that crying was a luxury a farm with one fewer pair of hands couldn't afford this morning, and she's holding to that decision through visible effort.

@Aveline: Good. You found each other first. That matters more than either of you probably realizes yet. Well. Today, then.
narrativeVariants.flags.civilian_departure_mood == 'alone':
Your mother, Aveline, finds you sitting alone, and doesn't immediately fill the silence the way she usually would - just sits down beside you for a moment first, before finally speaking. She doesn't cry. She decided a long time ago that crying was a luxury a farm with one fewer pair of hands couldn't afford this morning, and she's holding to that decision through visible effort.

@Aveline: I'll let you have the quiet a moment longer, if you need it. But the day's not going to wait much past that. Today, then.

narrative:
Elder Maren is waiting at the crossroads shrine on your way out, which can't be coincidence - she's timed farewells like this before, for others, and knows exactly which morning to be standing where.

@Elder Maren: The road doesn't care what you were at home. Farmer's child, blacksmith's apprentice, doesn't matter out there. It only cares what you do with what you knew before you leave it. Don't forget Aldenmoor taught you anything just because Aldenmoor is small.

narrative:
Joss is leaning on the village gatepost like he's been there for hours, which, knowing him, he probably has. You've known him since before either of you could reliably tie your own boots, and he's worn the exact same expression at every important goodbye the two of you have ever had - trying too hard to look like it doesn't matter.

@Joss: Figured someone should see you off who isn't going to cry about it. Your mother's got that covered for the whole village already.

narrative: The road out of Aldenmoor is one you've walked before, but only ever partway - to the mill, to the next farm over, never all the way to where it stops being a road you know by name. Every farmhouse you pass is a small, specific kind of familiar. You won't have that again for a long while, and some part of you is only now doing the arithmetic on what that actually costs.

narrative:
Your hands remember seed grain, wet earth, and the terrible arithmetic of a pantry in late winter. You did not leave home because ordinary life was beneath you. You left because ordinary people deserve someone who comes back when trouble starts.

The messenger's boots leave small crescents of mud across the inn floor where you've stopped to rest. They apologize for it twice. You remember doing the same thing when you were young and afraid that making a mess was worse than bringing bad news.

A messenger brings word of sick fields on the next road over. You are already packing before the sentence ends.

narrative: The first night you spend somewhere that isn't Aldenmoor, in any direction, arrives quietly and lands harder than you expected. No familiar creak of the house settling. No Nessa's breathing through the shared wall. Just your own fire, your own watch, and considerably more sky than you're used to noticing.
